candidateAssessment.concept: Korean language, literature and cultural media
candidateAssessment.assessment: UCR supplies literary, film, media, rhetoric and heritage methods, but no Korean-language instruction and no documented Korean literature, media, cultural tradition or material-heritage sequence. Filling 23 non-PPD places with generic methods would remove the Korean object that defines the direction.

candidateAssessment.concept: Korean history, society and the divided peninsula
candidateAssessment.assessment: Modern history, empire, sociology and qualitative methods are genuine analytic foundations, but the documented course content does not provide Korean history, the division of the peninsula, North Korean communism, South Korean capitalism or sustained social-science study of Korea.

candidateAssessment.concept: Korea in regional politics and economic development
candidateAssessment.assessment: Comparative politics, international relations and international macroeconomics supply transferable frameworks. They do not offer a Korea- or East Asia-centred politics and development sequence, so expanding them to a full programme would become generic international studies rather than a defensible response to the stated Korean Studies interest.

findings: Language/culture: Psycholinguistics supplies experimental acquisition, bilingualism and processing. Style & Meaning and literature supply textual inquiry, Film & Text supplies adaptation research, and documentary and media archaeology supply visual, archival and material methods. World Archaeology includes Asian artifacts, and Modern Art & Modern Museums supports critical curatorial study beyond Western narratives. None of these develops competence with Korean-language material or sustains Korean literature, cultural history or media as the advanced object.

History/society: Modern History and History of Empires contribute modernisation, migration, imperial comparison and source work, including Chinese imperial examples. Qualitative Research and Contemporary Social Theory contribute methods and public-sphere/civil-society study. Researching the American Century uses substantial historical inquiry within its current American subject. Media & Race supplies Asian-American exclusion and Japanese-American incarceration within American media and cultural history. Those bounded comparisons do not anchor a programme on Korea or its division.

Politics/development: Comparative Politics, International Relations and Peace & Conflict contribute institutional comparison, geopolitical case inquiry and peacebuilding. Public International Law and Comparative Constitutional Law provide legal and institutional analysis. International Macroeconomics models aggregate policy and international shocks. International Business & Governance analyzes market entry, trade and cross-border institutional differences. Private Law includes a Chinese comparison, in a different substantive field. No sustained Korean political economy is documented.

Combined challenge: a comparative programme on East Asian modernity, divided societies and cultural representation can use the above methods together. The strongest supported course mix would still devote most advanced study to US or other regional cases and general comparative tools. A student project could choose a Korean question, but topic freedom does not create the specialist learning progression or depth. The assessment depends on what the full curriculum teaches and the exact target interest, without imposing course-by-course equivalence or a minimum overlap count.
implementation: The supported external curriculum and reason are published. No UCR schedule, selected course-description text or alignment is exposed for this exception. The planning workbook was not used to infer academic no-match.
